toc.title: Buying a course on selling courses
What was in front of me the whole time

blocks.p: Desperation can bring us to some scary places. I was dysregulated and desperate, and I agreed to spend $9,000, which eventually led to a millionaire threatening me. I'm sharing this embarrassing story to normalize that desperation happens, and to tie it together with a few key lessons. This one is less about teaching Polyvagal Theory and more about me, and I'm curious whether you can relate.

Around October of 2022, my wife and I ran face first into some major financial concerns. Our careers made major, unexpected deviations from the path we thought we were on. A big old wrench got thrown into our system, and I'm not going to go into detail about it. Basically, the life we had planned for the next couple of years was not going to happen. If we were going to make it happen, we would have had to really sacrifice, and it would have come at the expense of our mental health and our physical health.

I don't mean that lightly. It was a very big deal. That sacrifice would have let us live in more financial comfort, but we were not willing to make it. So we made some very big career changes, and our combined annual income was cut by over half.

Our cozy little life was turned upside down, very literally overnight, and everything was up in the air. To tell you I was stressed is an understatement. There was a week or so where I didn't eat much. I knew I should eat. I brought food to work, and we had food in the house. I just wasn't hungry. I did eat, but not like I usually do, and I swear I lost about 10 pounds in that one week.

Was I in a defensive state? Yeah, definitely. There was some flight, but honestly, it was mostly fight. I had more aggression in my system, though it wasn't an aggressive, uncontrolled sort of fight. It was more motivation. It was pointed. I had purpose. There was a problem, I was dead set on solving it, and I believed in myself: "I can make this happen."

My mind had a singular focus: how to keep my family afloat through our financial turmoil. And it had a singular answer: use my business to make more money. Podcasting, therapy, course sales. How do I make more money doing this?

The problem is I had no idea how to do that. Not very well, at least. Historically, I've been terrible at selling my courses. I know the courses are amazing. I know they provide exactly what people want, which is help with self-regulation and getting unstuck. But in the world of entrepreneurship, the courses being amazing doesn't mean much if I don't know how to sell them.
So somewhere in the first week or so after my wife and I made this big decision together, I started to get desperate. My motivated fight energy turned into something else.

blocks.h: Buying a course on selling courses

blocks.p: This is when I decided it was time to buy a course for myself. Perfect timing, right? And what kind of course was I searching for? A course on how to sell courses, of course.

I went to YouTube to see who was out there selling what. I knew there were these business types, people who are really good at hustling and making money, who give out free information and then make an offer. I listened to what people were putting out and what their offers were, and I got exactly what I expected: skeevy, slimy salespeople who made me say, "Ugh, yuck."

But there was one person, who I will keep anonymous because they threatened to come after me with their millions of dollars. I felt like she was speaking directly to me. She understood my desperation. She understood my pain. She knew exactly what I needed, and wouldn't you know it, she had the answer, too.

The price wasn't mentioned in the YouTube video or on her website, but I scheduled a chat anyway to see if I was a good fit for the program. I knew it was going to be a lot of money. I didn't know how much, but I knew it was going to be a lot.

On the call, I spoke with one of her people. He seemed like a likable fellow. He made small talk at the beginning and asked where I was from. He wasn't overly aggressive, but he was obviously sending me through a scripted sequence of talking points. Even in that opening chat, I thought, "Ugh. You obviously don't care. You're going off a script."

I was aware of this, and I looked the other way. I told myself, "I suppose it's just normal in the world of business, and they have the skills that I don't. So who am I to question it? Do I want help or not?"
He asked me a few questions about my business and my motivation level, and apparently it all checked out, because he proclaimed that I'd be a great fit for their program. Huzzah.

He still didn't mention the price, so I told myself, "It's probably something like 10 grand. Crap, I can't afford this, but I also cannot do this on my own. I need what they have, and I'm going to suck it up. Something in my life has to change. I am going to make this work so my family can have a better life. I don't want to lose my house. I don't want to sell my stuff or take the kids out of the extracurricular activities that are so healthy for them, emotionally and socially."
Remember, story follows state. My mind was going some pretty extreme places.

So I asked him how much it cost. Very coolly, very calmly, with a wave of his hand like it was nothing, he said, "$8,600." I know for some people that is nothing, and good for them. For me, it's definitely something. A lot of something.
"Yeah, I don't have that," I told him.
"Well, how much do you have?" he asked. That felt a bit forward, but I answered, and he assured me the payments could be broken into four installments, for a total of $9,000.
"But what if I'm not able to pay that? I won't be taking money out of my family's account. This would come out of my business account. What happens if I'm not able to make the payments?"

He assured me, very assuredly, that once I was in the program, I'd be making money like so many people before me. And I said, "Yeah, that makes sense. And damn it, I'm betting on myself here. I'm not going to let anything get in my way."
He also tossed in this: "I mean, how hard is it really to come up with the money? You could pull from your family's account, borrow from somebody, or even put it on your credit card."

Yes, just like you, I saw that as a big red flag, and I ignored it. Why? Because I was desperate. Because they had what I needed, and I was in enough dysregulated fight energy to plow through anything and take any reassurance that was offered. So I said, "Fuck it. Let's do it." And that's how I put down a couple grand and committed to seven more.

So, am I rich beyond measure now? Was the course amazing? No, and no. Not for me, at least. I absolutely hated it. I went in with all guns blazing and gave it my best, most honest shot. But wow, was I a terrible fit.

It's really good for the person who wants to sell, sell, sell, then go to sleep and sell some more while they're asleep. It's for the person who wants to spend eight hours a day in DMs, which one of the lesson modules actually recommended. It's for the person who wants to script their conversations with their so-called avatars, get them on calls, and run them through a script. I felt gross about all of it, and it still feels icky saying it out loud.

After four days in the course, I emailed one of the leads and said, "I am not a good fit for this course." Then I groveled for my money back and to be cut loose from the agreement. I took full responsibility for my decision. I was in a contract and obliged to it, but I regretted the heck out of it. I said something like, "It's entirely on me. I made the decision to commit and pay the money, and I still will if I can't leave the program with a refund. But I'm hoping you'd be willing to refund what I put in and let me out of the agreement."

Being in that course was eating away at my stomach. It was like acid in my stomach, like it was twisting with intense anxiety. And honestly, embarrassment as well, and regret, and just feeling stupid. Lots of feelings.

That email set up a phone call with the lead. She tried to talk me into staying, and I explained why I wasn't a good fit. I kept repeating myself, because she wasn't quite getting it. I said numerous times, "I'm sure the course is great, and I see people in the group getting results. I just don't want to be a part of it. It's not the culture I'm looking to be part of, and the course design made no sense to me." It was convoluted and complex. There was a script for the script, and before you did that script you had to do something else, and it was click here and click there. I could not make heads or tails of it.

I don't think I'm a stupid person, but that course did not click for me at all. On top of that, there was a whole culture they were creating that I just couldn't be part of. I may not be very good at selling my own courses, but I can design one hell of a course, with the best of them. The people I bought it from knew how to sell, but their course design was terrible.

She really struggled to understand how I could want to back out. She said, "We don't give refunds," but that she'd get back to me after talking to their chief financial officer. While I waited, the regret and anxiety were gnawing away at me.

Later that day, I got an email explaining that they had no obligation to, but they would let me out of the contract minus some administrative fees, around 400 bucks. That's a lot of money, but I was ecstatic. I was getting most of what I put in back, and I was out. I felt like they did me a big favor.

The email was also very clear that I was not to share who they are or the fact that they gave me a refund. If I ever did, they would take legal action against me. Like they had broken some major rule just by giving me a refund. I thought, "Okay, cool. Not a problem. I will never share who this is." But also: you're this threatening about a refund?

It still strikes me as odd. If you have what you call a millionaire mindset, an abundance mindset, if you brag about the millions you're bringing in, why be this intense over a refund? It makes me wonder whether they truly have an abundance mindset or a scarcity mindset. Okay, I'm starting to get petty. But it was like they were clutching their money so tightly. Then again, I'm not a millionaire, so what do I know? Whatever. They let me out. Onward.

blocks.h: What was in front of me the whole time

blocks.p: What I ended up doing was finding something that was perfect for me, and I have no regrets. The weird thing is that this person was in front of me the whole time, and I don't know why I didn't think of him sooner, especially in that moment of desperation: Pat Flynn.

I'm not trying to plug him, and there's no affiliate link here. I'd been listening to his podcast for about a year. He was part of my weekly life. I was super aware of his credentials. I knew his story and what he offers. And for some reason, when I was desperate, I didn't think of him. It's really frustrating.

But that's where I turned, and it's been fantastic. He has really great courses, and I'm super happy there. I have a community and courses, and a lot of what I've built for myself has been modeled on what he does at Smart Passive Income.

So after all this, am I making a ton of money? No, not at all. At least not yet. I really believe I can do better, but I'm not there. In the meantime, what I am getting is connection with other people like me, people trying to build their businesses from the bottom up. I'm getting fantastic information. And I'm relearning the importance of connecting with my audience, knowing who that audience is, and providing for them as best I possibly can.
This wasn't just embarrassing story time. There are a few lessons here.

ol: Desperation is okay. Desperate decision making may not be. It's hard to notice you're desperate and turn it off. Fair enough. But it's okay to be desperate. Hold back on the decision making if you can. At the same time, you may make really razor-sharp decisions when you're in more of a fight state. That might be true. You'll have to check that for yourself, even if it's after the fact.

You might have what you need right in front of you. Pat Flynn knows his stuff, and he was right in front of me every week for a year, and I didn't think of him. So look at what you have in your life. There might be an answer there for you when it comes to your self-development or your trauma relief.

Plan ahead, lay the foundations, and build from there. We already know that, right? Plan ahead as best you can, and lay those foundations as solidly as you can now. For me, yes, I want to sell more courses, but I really want to make sure I'm providing value and deepening my connections with the people I serve, especially my course students, and that I'm absolutely nailing what they need.

Intent matters a lot. The practices I learned in that course I hated aren't bad in and of themselves. Giving away free content and then offering a course is pretty normal. I hated the way they did the scheduled chat, but I offer chats about my courses now too. The difference is that there's no script. I will never ask for payment during one of those chats. I will never suggest you take money from your family or put it on a credit card. That's ridiculous. I'm there purely to answer questions and make sure you have every piece of information you need before you make a decision. Same practice, different intent.

blocks.p: I hope this has been helpful, and I hope it's been normalizing.
